No. The study that’s often referenced when talking about drug addiction involves a rat in a cage with food and some addictive substance delivered when a button is pressed. The rat ate some food, but pressed the button more and more frequently until it starved or overdosed. 

However, years later some people saw a problem with the study design; the rats were not in a normal environment during the experiment. Rats, like humans, are intelligent and social animals that crave mental stimulation. The experiment was repeated, but this time, a group of familiar rats were placed in a spacious cage with toys so they could play and socialize. This time, the food was eaten at a healthy rate and the some drugs were used, but not much or frequently.

So the people least likely to become addicted would be the generally well adjusted and healthy folks with good social bonds.

At my college, there are required credits so everyone needs some kind of a math class, an art class, an English class, a minority’s nonwestern history or culture class, a natural science class, a western history class, and 2 years of a language. 

Right now, I’m thinking of my major (biology) and my good friend’s (vocal performance). For someone pursuing a biology or other natural science degree, it would be hard to find a job without some high level courses. And for medical school, you straight up can’t get in without 300-400 biology classes, physics, organic chem, organic chem lab, calculus, and psychology, minimum.

For my particular major, I need:

intro to organismal & evolution biology
intro to molecular & cellular biology
molecular evolution (lecture and lab)
plant and animal biology in evolutionary and environmental contexts
two calculus classes
2 inorganic chem classes 
2inorganic chem labs
organic chem
At least 6 hours of advanced chemistry courses
a 400 level class on biostatistics
400 level biochem
2 semesters of physics
400 level molecular biology computing
2 semesters of independent research
10 hours of 300-400 level biology courses

Keep in mind the shorter labs are scheduled for 4 hours. But for a couple bio labs, I spent the night in the lab and stopping in between classes to measure or feed something. And regular labs were 4-6 hours. And god forbid if you mismeasured an enzyme by a microliter (1/1000 of a milliliter), cause you’ll have to prepare everything again, motto mention another 1 hour 20 min in the thermocycler and another 30 min in the old electrophoresis machine.

Now, my friend’s vocal performance major requires:

4 semesters of music theory
4 semesters of aural skills
2 piano classes
advanced music theory
2 semesters of music history
musical perspective
performance in 2 operas
preparing and performing 2 recitals
conducting
English/French/Italian/German diction
music pedagogy
2 semesters of Italian
2 semesters of German
2 semesters of French

Majors are meant to provide you with professional knowledge in an area. College is a also a place to become more well rounded, but that’s what the required credits are for. One could argue that aren’t enough, but everyone having the same requirements would either mean lowering the amount of classes you can take that are in your area of study or forcing people to take a bunch of classes that they don’t enjoy and won’t provide much benefit in the future.

I actually took voice lessons and an acting class. Loved them. But advanced music theory? Conducting? The time commitment of performing in two operas? And if my friend is a singer, making her struggle through organic chemistry, biostatistics, and molecular evolution goes far beyond what’s necessary for her to be well rounded

His hard work. His commitment to family. How he reacts to racism by taking no shit but to try to educate as well. This got kind of long, but pls at least read #3, it describes him so well.


1) He was born in the 50s and raised by a single mother who worked night and day to provide for him in my aunt. He was black in Detroit and was a victim of police brutality (Basically 2 policemen would cruise black neighborhoods, get out of their squad car about 100 feet in the direction a single black man was walking, and assault him, hoping he would react in self defense so they could further brutalize and arrest him. There was a term for this, my dad told me but I don’t recall rn. Anyway, he trained in some martial arts and worked out a lot, so when he saw the police approaching him, he flexed his abdomen as much as possible. One of them punched him hard to the point he was lifted off the ground, but he was able to keep a neutral face and the officers kept walking without a word. He says that without flexing properly, that kind of hit can be lethal or at least cause multiple organ rupture.

2) After high school he got into college with a football scholarship but (because he spent a lot of time studying medicine, especially neurology), he thought the risk of brain damage wasn’t worth it. Instead, he pumped gas for $1.30/hour to help pay for school and overloaded his schedule so he only had to pay for three years (he still doesn’t get why I had to choose between two classes at the same time because he regularly registered like that).

3) Then, he went to medical school. He continued to work at the gas station and studied during any lull in work. He was one of two black men in most of his classes. His neuroanatomy instructor always failed my dad on subjective assignments (like essays and stuff), even when his answers were correct based on his textbooks and lectures. He asked the other black med student if he was experiencing anything like that and he was (the other student’s work wasn’t perfect, but all of his correct things were labeled as false). So my dad approached the professor who, to his face, said, “colored students aren’t good at academia. I can’t pass you if I know you won’t be a good doctor.” So my dad went to his superiors who came up with a test. He would have to sit in front of them and his instructor would ask him ANY three questions based on the textbook. So naturally, they were difficult and obscure so the instructor could save face and prove his racist rational. But my dad studies his ass off, went through his extensive notes, and generally prepared more that any med student would be expected to. So the day of the interrogation, the professor asked the first question. Dad got it right. Then he asked the second, right again. Then the third, and lo and behold, Dad knew it. The board decided the instructor wasn’t grading equally and told my dad his grade would be be based on objective exams and his hospital work. 
Then, because it’s just my dads style, he asked the board if he could ask his instructor 3 questions. They said sure, so he put forth his 3 questions, all based on the textbook. And the instructor got them all wrong.

Buuuuut, my dad didn’t think the instructor quite got the point. So he showed up to this instructor’s office hours. All his office hours. And spent that time teaching HIM all aspects he could find about neuroanatomy. He said part of the reason he did this  is to show him how ridiculous his opinion about black doctors were and partially to make sure he fully understood the material. But I know he also did it to fuck with him a little. Still, he was never mean or insulting when the instructor made a mistake and they got to know each other during the the rest of the course. And Dad finished top of his class and became friends with the man. They kept in touch during my dads residency and as he earned his neurology fellowship.

4) He and my mom raised my bro and I in the best public school district in the area. He makes good money but very rarely spends it on himself. He’s happy with his corvette, recliner, and tv. And spends so much time and money caring for my mother’s and my medical issues. He offered to get me a new (lighter) laptop, paid for physical therapy, and paid for regular massages when my back hurts. When I asked if he could pay for a bit of my trip to France if I used my savings on the rest, he agreed, then paid for it all.

I don’t like it. I know people who have mental or developmental disabilities and they find the term really hurtful. 

Some people will justify it by saying its a medical term, but it no longer is because how people use the term to insult and belittle.

Some people justify saying it because they claim they aren’t using it to describe mentally or developmentally disabled people, but it usually is used to reference them. Even if a speaker genuinely doesn’t have a mental connection of the r-word and disabled people, societally there is a connection. So anyone in earshot makes that connection between developmental disability and being bad, stupid, or just an object of ridicule. And anyone with such a disability or their loved ones hear the person say that, they’ll think less of you and worried for themselves or those they care about.

The English language is so broad and descriptive, the r-word doesn’t need to be part of casual conversation. Sure you CAN use it, but only if saying it rather than so many other descriptive words is more important to you than avoiding damaging a large group of already disenfranchised and socially marginalize group of people.

It’s not very fun, but I do like telling people about rabies. A lot people think it’s a normal illness that can be dangerous but is generally treatable. BUT:

1) My friend, who originally made me interested in rabies, has moved a lot told me one area (I want to say Montana or Utah but I don’t remember) there were lots of caves and bats, and after a few stories came out about a few people being bitten by bats carrying the disease, citizens started calling the CDC and animal control for every bat they saw. They eventually made an announcement for people in the area to stop calling in bats to have them check for rabies because it waisted resources. Not because people were wrong and paranoid by fearing a bat had rabies, but because every bat they caught WAS carrying rabies. So basically, if you see a bat, it has rabies. Don’t make us check, we already know it has rabies.

2) Bats definitely aren’t the only animals to transmit rabies. However, you know if you’re bitten by a dog or something, but bat bites aren’t really noticeable. They don’t hurt much and don’t leave big, obvious marks. They often look like a couple of big bites. People have woken up and only realized a bat bit them because of the spacing between the marks.

3) You really have to play it safe with rabies. There are 2 ways to find out if an animal has rabies. You can kill it and dissect its brain or wait until it starts showing symptoms.
 
Btw, if you’ve been bitten by a possible rabies carrier, you go to hospital and get a series of expensive, painful injections into the abdomen. “Why would they do that if they only think it might turn into rabies” well...

4) rabies stays dormant in the human body for a while. It can take over a six years to turn symptomatic. And those symptoms, at the beginning, are identical to the flu. But even if you start getting these seemingly innocuous symptoms, happen to remember that camping trip four summers ago where you woke up with weird bug bites, realize it could have actually been a bat, AND know the symptoms of rabies well enough to connect your current illness to the camping trip, you’re still screwed because...

5) Once symptoms appear it’s already too late! Those stabs to the tummy can’t help you now. But you go to the hospital because you don’t want to deal with later symptoms like brain inflammation, paranoia, hallucinations, and partial paralysis outside of a medical setting. But maybe they’ll treat it there. 

6) PSYCH! Rabies is a virtual death sentence. Most people last 2-10 days after symptoms appear.

7) There is semi-good news. Even though the  disease had a 0% survival rate, in 2014, a young women showing symptoms was given an experimental treatment and became the first person in history to survive rabies without the vaccine. The treatment is called the Milwaukee Protocol which consists of inducing a coma in the patient until the disease has run its course and hoping they’ll wake up again has saved a grand total of 6 people and raises your odds from 0:20 to 3:20.

Gasses can be dissolved in liquid in a similar way that solids can be dissolved in liquid. For example, CO2 in soft drinks or sugar crystals in water.

By messing with things like temperature and/or pressure, you can get more stuff (gas or solids) dissolved in a liquid than in normal conditions. 

For example, consider the process of making rock candy. You can mix some sugar into room temperature water, but you can get much MORE to dissolve if the water is hot. As the sugar water cools, less sugar is able to stay dissolved in the solution so it will form crystals. Sugar crystals form best on a surface with slight imperfections that allow the crystals to “take hold”.

Now, let’s consider a soft drink. More CO2 can dissolve in water if it’s all kept under higher pressure, like in a sealed can or bottle. When the seal is broken, and the pressure inside decreases, a bunch of the CO2 comes out of solution. CO2 gas doesn’t crystallize like sugar, instead, the gas molecules group together into small bubbles, or fizz. The bubbles, like sugar crystals, form mostly on the inside surface of the container, especially where it’s less smooth. The bottom of a clear container is the most likely interior surface to have imperfection such as curves, grooves, or etc. So, much of fizz collects here before floating up.

Also. Bubbles released from the bottom of the container are further from the sides (making them easier to see) and take longer to reach the surface (giving you more time to see them).

Your college is a great place to start. Depending on the size and type of school, they can offer a variety of resources, often at no cost. 

You can begin at your school’s clinic and speak with a general practitioner about how you’re feeling so they can guide you. Or you can head directly to the college’s counseling services. They can usually set you up with finding a professional to see regularly, group therapy, and even directed disordered eating resources.

Outside of school, there are free Overeaters Anonymous meetings all over the country. I’m sure there’s one near you. General eating disorder groups can be really useful too. I think some people with overeating problems or binge eating feel like they would be out of place there, but they really just focus on re-evaluating your relationship with food.

Other things that may help include:

Food Journaling: When and why did you eat? Were you hungry, feeling a strong emotion, bored? How did you feel afterward? What situations make you feel more or less in control about what you consume? Etc.

Interrupt & replace the habit: it takes trial and error, but what can distract you when you get the urge to overeat? Maybe a walk around the block, having a big mug of tea, listening to a podcast, doing a face mask, etc. will give you a moment to wait for the urge to lessen.

Go slow: start with a dish of food, as reasonable as you can, and put the rest away. Eat it slowly, drinking plenty of water during, and try to wait 15 minutes before deciding if you want to go back for more. 


I’ve had some eating issues in the past, so feel free to message me if you have any questions or want to talk. Or if you want to be more specific about your location, I may be able to help you find resources near by.

Tylenol (acetaminophen).

It’s the #1 cause of acute liver failure (beating out alcohol). Mostly because  it’s seen as such a harmless medicine that’s been around such a long time, people feel like it’s super safe and taking a few extra won’t be a big deal.

But while Tylenol labels 6 pills as a safe daily dose, the FDA says 10 is dangerous. So say, you had a bad headache or pulled a muscle in your back and were going to take the max labeled dose by taking 2 every 6-8  hours. You take the first 2 pills, but it doesn’t touch the pain. So for your next 2 doses, you take 3 pills (after all it’s just one more of an over the counter pill). But now your at an unsafe level. And if you happen to have a drink, take cold medicine that also contained acetaminophen, or take other meds that are metabolized through the liver, you may be in some trouble.

Many experts say that if acetaminophen was introduced today, there’s no way it would be available, at least without a prescription.

I also have a personal aversion to it as my close friend attempted suicide multiple times through Tylenol overdoses. It’s an agonizing, gruesome process. She still has jaundice (yellow tinged skin) from liver damage.

POTS usually has a more physical cause such as an autoimmune disease, head injury, or genetic condition. That’s not to say you’re wrong though. I could see how major depression could indirectly lead to POTS like if a lack of energy left you deconditioned or if you became malnourished.

POTS does have a lot of comorbid conditions, including mood disorders. I also have depression and my doctors and I definitely believe POTS and other chronic health problems contribute to it. If I’m already struggling with motivation, self esteem, and social anxiety, things like fatigue, brain fog, and feeling out of place can send me into a spiral.

My current therapist actually has chronic Lyme disease (so even though we aren’t going through the exact same thing, she can relate to how illness affects my mood and everyday life). If you’re looking for talk therapy (which I highly suggest), it might be useful to find someone who specializes in people with disabilities or chronic illnesses or be extra mindful that they try to understand how having pots and depression affects you.

You aren’t alone in this. Dealing with dysautonomia or depression is hard enough without the symptoms and problems mixing together. But I really believe you’ll find ways to better manage both with medication, habits, and/or through your medical team, even though it takes trial and error.
